title: Operational Resource Utilisation Practices in a Grain Handling and Storage Operation

lessons.title: Analysing resource utilisation across the operation
lessons.html:
A management-level view

At NQF level 6 you are expected to evaluate how well the whole operation, often a group of depots, uses its resources and to lead improvements with measurable financial results. The work takes place in a real operation with your mentor or line manager.

Framework for analysis

ResourceUtilisation measureTypical questions
Storage capacityAverage and peak percentage filled, revenue per tonne of capacityAre some depots full while others are under-used? Should bunkers be used less?
Handling equipmentThroughput, availability, OEE, cost per tonne handledWhere are the bottlenecks? What is downtime costing?
DryersFuel per tonne of water removed, hours runAre dryers drying below target moisture? Is fuel the right type?
EnergykWh per tonne by depot, maximum demandWhich depots are outliers and why?
PeopleTonnes per labour hour, overtime percentage, seasonal versus permanent mixIs overtime caused by breakdowns or poor rostering?
StockShrink, variancesWhich losses are normal and which are controllable?
CapitalReturn on investment, age and condition of assetsWhich assets should be refurbished, replaced or retired?

Benchmarking

Compare depots against each other and over several seasons. Normalise data where needed, for example per tonne handled or per tonne of water removed, so that depots of different sizes and moisture conditions are compared fairly. Look for best practice in the top performers and transfer it.

Cost of losses

Express every loss in rand. For example, if shrink is 0.3 percentage points above the accepted level on 150 000 tonnes of maize, that is 450 tonnes of grain; multiplied by the current market price, this often exceeds the annual cost of better weighbridge controls, moisture meter verification and spillage repairs. Financial framing helps management prioritise.

lessons.title: Leading resource optimisation initiatives
lessons.html:
Selecting initiatives

Choose initiatives based on value, cost, risk and ease of implementation. A simple matrix of impact versus effort helps: start with high-impact, low-effort actions (quick wins) while planning larger projects.

Examples of initiatives

  • Storage optimisation – redistribute intake among depots to reduce bunker use and associated quality risk; align out-loading with storage risk.
  • Energy – install aeration controllers, variable speed drives on large fans, power factor correction, or solar PV with load-shifting; manage maximum demand.
  • Drying – automate moisture control to avoid over-drying; maintain burners; insulate and seal.
  • Maintenance – move from breakdown to condition-based maintenance on elevators and dryers, reducing peak-season downtime.
  • Labour – multi-skill staff, adjust roster patterns to truck arrival profiles, reduce overtime.
  • Stock control – tighten weighbridge and moisture controls, monthly reconciliations and security improvements.

Business case

For capital initiatives prepare a business case: problem, options, costs, expected savings, payback period, risks, and implementation plan. Consider safety, legal compliance and client service, not only cost. For example, replacing an old elevator may be justified by dust explosion risk reduction as much as by throughput.

Implementation and change leadership

  1. Agree objectives and measures with management.
  2. Appoint a project owner and team, including operators.
  3. Communicate the reasons and expected benefits to staff.
  4. Implement in phases where possible; pilot at one depot first.
  5. Measure results against baseline and adjust.
  6. Standardise successful practices across depots and update procedures.

Reporting

Report utilisation performance and initiative results to senior management regularly: savings achieved, KPIs improved, lessons learnt and next steps. Keep the report focused on decisions management needs to make.

Key points

  • Evaluate utilisation of storage, equipment, dryers, energy, people, stock and capital.
  • Benchmark depots using normalised data and transfer best practice.
  • Express losses in rand to prioritise action.
  • Build business cases that include safety, compliance and service as well as cost.
  • Pilot, measure, standardise and report results to management.
